I coach sales teams in six countries, and when I listen to a recorded call, I am not listening for perfect English. I am listening for the shape of the call. A good call has five parts, and the order matters. First, two minutes of rapport and a short agenda, so the other person knows where you are going. Then questions, many more questions than you think, before you say a single word about the product. Then a short explanation, connected to what they just told you. Then the objection, because there is always one, and the best salespeople ask for it instead of hiding from it. And finally, a next step with a date and a name. Not we will be in touch. A date and a name. If a call has those five parts, I do not care about a few grammar mistakes. If it does not have them, perfect grammar will not save it.

Last year we chose a Brazilian vendor over two American ones, and people asked me why. The product was good, but so were the others. What made the difference was the first call. Their head of sales did not start with a presentation. He asked me how our month-end close worked, and then he asked again, and he wrote it down. When I said something he did not understand, he did not pretend. He said, sorry, could you say that again, and then he repeated it in his own words to check. His English was not perfect, and it did not matter. When I raised the price, he did not panic. He asked what the price was compared with, and he came back with a trade-off. And at the end he gave me a date for the next call before I could ask. That is what a partner looks like, in any language.
